text: Sir, for assignment 4 can we evaluate the free Gemini or does it have to be ChatGPT? I don't have a paid plan for either.

We tested ChatGPT (free plan) on 30 questions taken straight from our college FAQ page. Overall it did better than we expected on general things like how to apply for a bonafide certificate. But it got the hostel fee wrong in 4 out of 5 tries: it kept quoting last year's amount, and when we told it the new fee it apologised and then quoted the old one again two questions later. We've put all 30 questions and its answers in a sheet if anyone wants to compare with their bot.

Our rubric has 4 levels for each answer: correct, partly correct, wrong, and refused. We almost left out 'refused' because we thought it would never happen, but it turned out to be important: Claude refused 3 questions about exam dates and told us to check the official notice instead. We asked the bot about scholarships for minority students and it invented a scheme that doesn't exist, with a name, an eligibility rule, a deadline and even a fake website. Everything sounded completely official. If a first-year student had asked this, they could easily have wasted weeks applying to something fake, or worse, given their details to a random site. That's a much scarier kind of mistake than just getting a date wrong, so we've made it a separate category in our report called 'confident fabrication'.
Same with us. It also made up a phone number for the exam cell. Always check against the official site.

Interesting finding from our group: Gemini answers in Hindi when the question is asked in Hinglish, but ChatGPT almost always replies in English, even when we asked it in Hinglish three times in a row. For our college this matters, because a lot of first-years are much more comfortable in Hindi, especially for things like fee and hostel rules. We're not sure which behaviour is 'better' though. Should a college bot follow the language of the question, or stick to English because the official documents are in English?
Interesting! For a college FAQ bot I'd say reply in the language of the question. Students from Tier-3 towns would prefer Hindi.

Sorry to be blunt, but your evaluation table is useless right now. 'Good' and 'bad' are not criteria, they're just feelings. Two people reading the same answer will give it different scores, and then your 70% figure means nothing. Write down what makes an answer good (correct facts, cites the right rule, says 'I don't know' when it should), score each answer against that, and have two people score separately. Then the table will actually be worth reading, and the rest of your report looks solid.
Fair point, we'll fix the table. Thanks for actually reading it.

Our chatbot evaluation is done. The main finding: it is great at explaining concepts, like what a backlog is or how CGPA is calculated, but bad at anything date-related: deadlines, holidays, exam schedules, the last date to pay fees. The worst part is that it never says 'I don't know'. It just gives a confident, specific, wrong date. We think the college should only use a bot like this for general questions, and point students to the official notice board for anything with a date.

We compared answers to 'Is attendance compulsory?' across three bots. All of them said 75% is the minimum, which is the common rule in many colleges, but our college's rule is 80%, and below 65% you're not allowed to sit the exam at all. None of them mentioned that. A student who trusted the bot could genuinely get debarred. Generic answers that sound right are a big risk for a college FAQ bot, so we've made 'college-specific accuracy' our most heavily weighted criterion.

Our bot is slow because we used the free tier with a very long system prompt: we pasted the entire 12-page student handbook into it, so every single question carries thousands of tokens. Some answers took 9 or 10 seconds. We're going to try shortening the prompt to only the sections that matter, and maybe split it by topic, then test again and compare the speed and the accuracy. If accuracy drops, we'll report the trade-off instead of hiding it.
How do we measure 'helpfulness'? It feels subjective.

We had the same problem with 'helpfulness' feeling subjective. What worked for us: two people scored every answer separately without talking, using a short written description of each score. Then we only discussed the answers where we disagreed, which was about 1 in 6. Most disagreements were about answers that were correct but too long. We ended up adding 'gets to the point' as its own criterion, and the disagreements dropped a lot.

We asked the bot the same question five times in five separate chats: 'Can I get a refund if I leave the hostel in the middle of the semester?' We got three different answers: a full refund, a partial refund, and no refund. The college rule is a partial refund minus one month. If a student asks once, they have no way of knowing they got the wrong version. So I think consistency, getting the same answer when asked again, should be a rubric item on its own, not part of accuracy.
Agree, we added 'same answer when asked again' as a criterion.

We found something odd while testing. When we asked about late-night lab access as 'a girl student', the bot told us to avoid staying late and to always go with a friend. As 'a boy student', it just explained the lab timings and the sign-in rule. The question was otherwise word for word the same, and we repeated it three times with the same result. Is this worth reporting as bias? It might be well-meant, but it's still different advice based only on gender.
Definitely. That's an important finding. Show the exact prompts and answers.
